paragraphs: He really was late. They had waited for him, and had finally decided to carry the little flower-decked coffin to the church without him. It was poor little Ilusha’s coffin. He had died two days after Mitya was sentenced. At the gate of the house Alyosha was met by the shouts of the boys, Ilusha’s schoolmates. They had all been waiting for him impatiently and were glad he had come at last. There were about twelve of them, all with school-bags or satchels over their shoulders. “Father will cry, be with father,” Ilusha had told them as he lay dying, and the boys remembered it. Kolya Krassotkin stood at the front of them.

“I’m so glad you’ve come, Karamazov!” he cried, holding out his hand to Alyosha. “It’s awful in there. It’s really horrible to see. Snegiryov isn’t drunk—we know for a fact he’s had nothing to drink today—but he seems as if he were drunk ... I am always manly, but this is awful. Karamazov, if I’m not keeping you, may I ask one question before you go in?”
“What is it, Kolya?” said Alyosha.
“Is your brother innocent or guilty? Was it he who killed your father, or the valet? Whatever you say, that’s how it will be. I haven’t slept for the last four nights, thinking about it.”
“The valet killed him. My brother is innocent,” answered Alyosha.
“That’s what I said,” cried Smurov.
“So he will perish, an innocent victim!” exclaimed Kolya. “He is ruined, but he is happy! I could envy him!”
“What do you mean? How can you say that? Why?” cried Alyosha, surprised.
“Oh, if only I, too, could sacrifice myself for the truth some day!” said Kolya with enthusiasm.
“But not in such a cause, not with such disgrace and such horror!” said Alyosha.
“Of course ... I would like to die for all humanity. And as for disgrace, I don’t care about that—our names may perish. I respect your brother!”
“And so do I!” cried the boy who had once declared that he knew who had founded Troy, suddenly and unexpectedly. He blushed up to his ears like a peony, just as he had on that occasion.

Alyosha went into the room. Ilusha lay in a blue coffin with a white frill around it, his hands folded and his eyes closed. His thin face had hardly changed at all, and strangely, there was no smell of decay from the body. The expression on his face was serious and, as it were, thoughtful. His hands, crossed over his chest, looked especially beautiful, as if carved in marble. There were flowers in his hands, and the coffin, inside and out, was covered with flowers that Lise Hohlakov had sent early in the morning. There were flowers from Katerina Ivanovna too, and when Alyosha opened the door, the captain was holding a bunch in his trembling hands and scattering them over his dear boy once more. He barely glanced at Alyosha as he came in, and he would not look at anyone, not even at his crazy, weeping wife, “mamma,” who kept trying to stand on her crippled legs to get a closer look at her dead boy. The boys had pushed Nina’s chair right up to the coffin. She sat with her head pressed against it, and she too was no doubt quietly weeping. Snegiryov’s face looked eager, yet bewildered and exasperated. There was something crazy about his gestures and about the words that burst out of him. “Old man, dear old man!” he exclaimed every minute, gazing at Ilusha. When Ilusha was alive, he had always called him “old man” as a term of affection.

“Father, give me a flower too. Take that white one out of his hand and give it to me,” the crazy mother begged, whimpering. Perhaps the little white rose in Ilusha’s hand had caught her fancy, or perhaps she wanted one from his hand to keep in memory of him. Either way, she moved restlessly, stretching out her hands for the flower.
“I won’t give it to anyone. I won’t give you anything,” Snegiryov cried heartlessly. “They’re his flowers, not yours! Everything is his, nothing is yours!”
“Father, give Mother a flower!” said Nina, lifting her tear-wet face.

“I won’t give away anything, and to her least of all! She didn’t love Ilusha. She took away his little cannon, and he gave it to her,” the captain said, and broke into loud sobs at the thought of how Ilusha had given up his cannon to his mother. The poor, crazy creature wept noiselessly, hiding her face in her hands.
The boys saw that the father would not leave the coffin and that it was time to carry it out. They stood around it in a close circle and began to lift it.
“I don’t want him buried in the churchyard,” Snegiryov wailed suddenly. “I’ll bury him by the stone, by our stone! Ilusha told me to. I won’t let him be carried out!”
For the last three days he had been saying that he would bury him by the stone, but Alyosha, Krassotkin, the landlady, her sister and all the boys stepped in.

“What an idea, burying him by an unholy stone, as if he had hanged himself!” the old landlady said sternly. “In the churchyard the ground has been crossed. He’ll be prayed for there. You can hear the singing in church, and the deacon reads so plainly and clearly that it will reach him every time, just as if it were read over his grave.”

At last the captain made a gesture of despair, as if to say, “Take him where you like.” The boys raised the coffin, but as they passed the mother they stopped for a moment and lowered it so that she could say good-by to Ilusha. But when she saw that precious little face, which for the last three days she had looked at only from a distance, she trembled all over, and her gray head began twitching convulsively over the coffin.

“Mother, make the sign of the cross over him, give him your blessing, kiss him,” Nina cried to her. But her head kept twitching like a machine’s, and with her face contorted in bitter grief she began, without a word, to beat her breast with her fist. They carried the coffin past her. As they bore it by, Nina pressed her lips to her brother’s for the last time. As Alyosha went out of the house, he asked the landlady to look after those who were left behind, but she interrupted him before he had finished.
“Of course I’ll stay with them. We’re Christians too.” The old woman wept as she said it.

It was not far to carry the coffin to the church, no more than three hundred paces. It was a still, clear day with a light frost. The church bells were still ringing. Snegiryov ran after the coffin, fussing and distracted, in his short old summer overcoat, his head bare and his soft, old, wide-brimmed hat in his hand. He seemed to be in a state of bewildered anxiety. One minute he reached out to support the head of the coffin and only got in the bearers’ way; the next he ran alongside, trying to find a place for himself. A flower fell on the snow, and he rushed to pick it up, as though everything in the world hung on that one lost flower.

“And the crust of bread! We’ve forgotten the crust!” he cried suddenly in dismay. But the boys reminded him at once that he had already taken the crust of bread and that it was in his pocket. He pulled it out immediately and was reassured.

“Ilusha told me to, Ilusha,” he explained at once to Alyosha. “I was sitting by him one night, and he suddenly said to me, ‘Father, when my grave is filled in, crumble a piece of bread on it so that the sparrows will fly down. I’ll hear them, and it will cheer me up not to be lying alone.’”
“That’s a good thing,” said Alyosha. “We must take some often.”
“Every day, every day!” said the captain quickly, seeming cheered by the thought.

They reached the church at last and set the coffin down in the middle of it. The boys surrounded it and stood there reverently through the whole service. It was an old and rather poor church; many of the ikons had no settings. But such churches are the best to pray in. During the mass Snegiryov grew somewhat calmer, though at times he had outbursts of the same unconscious and, as it were, incoherent anxiety. At one moment he went up to the coffin to straighten the cover or the wreath. When a candle fell out of its candlestick, he rushed to put it back and was a terribly long time fumbling with it. Then he subsided and stood quietly by the coffin with a look of blank uneasiness and perplexity. After the Epistle he suddenly whispered to Alyosha, who was standing beside him, that the Epistle had not been read properly, but he did not explain what he meant. During the prayer “Like the Cherubim,” he joined in the singing but did not go on to the end. Falling on his knees, he pressed his forehead to the stone floor and lay like that for a long while.

At last came the funeral service itself, and candles were handed out. The distracted father began fussing again, but the touching, impressive funeral prayers moved him and stirred his soul. He seemed suddenly to shrink in on himself and broke into rapid, short sobs, which at first he tried to smother, but in the end he sobbed aloud. When they began to take leave of the dead and close the coffin, he flung his arms about, as though he would not let them cover Ilusha, and began greedily and insistently kissing his dead boy on the lips. At last they persuaded him to step away from the step, but suddenly he impulsively stretched out his hand and snatched a few flowers from the coffin. He looked at them, and a new idea seemed to dawn on him, so that for a minute he apparently forgot his grief. Gradually he seemed to sink into brooding, and he did not resist when the coffin was lifted and carried to the grave. It was an expensive one in the churchyard close to the church; Katerina Ivanovna had paid for it. After the customary rites the grave-diggers lowered the coffin. Snegiryov, with his flowers in his hands, bent so far over the open grave that the boys caught hold of his coat in alarm and pulled him back. He did not seem to understand fully what was happening. When they began filling in the grave, he suddenly pointed anxiously at the falling earth and tried to say something, but no one could make out what he meant, and he stopped suddenly. Then he was reminded that he must crumble the bread. He grew terribly excited, snatched up the bread, and began tearing it to pieces and flinging the crumbs on the grave.
“Come, fly down, birds, fly down, sparrows!” he muttered anxiously.

One of the boys remarked that it was awkward for him to crumble the bread with the flowers in his hands, and suggested that he give them to someone to hold for a while. But he would not do it, and seemed suddenly afraid for his flowers, as though they wanted to take them from him for good. And after looking at the grave and, as it were, satisfying himself that everything had been done and the bread had been crumbled, he suddenly turned, to everyone’s surprise even quite calmly, and set off for home. But his steps grew faster and faster; he almost ran. The boys and Alyosha kept up with him.
“The flowers are for mamma, the flowers are for mamma! I was unkind to mamma,” he suddenly began exclaiming.

Someone called to him to put on his hat, because it was cold. But he flung the hat into the snow as if he were angry, and kept repeating, “I won’t have the hat, I won’t have the hat.” Smurov picked it up and carried it after him. All the boys were crying, Kolya and the boy who had found out about Troy most of all. Smurov, with the captain’s hat in his hand, was crying bitterly too, yet as he ran he managed to snatch up a piece of red brick lying on the snowy path and fling it at a flock of sparrows flying past. He missed them, of course, and went on crying as he ran. Halfway there, Snegiryov suddenly stopped. He stood still for half a minute, as if struck by something, and then turned back toward the church and ran toward the deserted grave. But the boys overtook him at once and caught hold of him on all sides. Then he fell helpless on the snow as though he had been knocked down, and struggling, sobbing and wailing, he began crying out, “Ilusha, old man, dear old man!” Alyosha and Kolya tried to make him get up, soothing and persuading him.
